column4: The section's worldly companion mocks the believer for affirming resurrection; this companion asks whether the speaker believes they will be judged (أَئِنَّكَ لَمِنَ الْمُصَدِّقِينَ), making denial the first edge of the later rescue scene.
The section quotes the companion's mockery in 37:52; this next question spells out its resurrection-denial, explaining why seeing him in the Fire answers the very claim he mocked.
The section's man looks down to see his former companion; this question, هل أنتم مطلعون, is the scene's invitation to look and directly sets up that downward sight.
The section's believer looks down and sees his former companion in the middle of Hell; this ayah narrates that very look and sight (فَاطَّلَعَ فَرَآهُ فِي سَوَاءِ الْجَحِيمِ).

The section says his friend nearly rolled him into ruin; the speaker says كِدْتَ لَتُرْدِينِ, from the same root ر د ي as source-section 92:11 تَرَدَّى, linking the friend's influence to the later plunge.

The section contrasts no human favor owed with one saving grace from the Lord; here the saved man says his Lord's favor kept him from being brought to punishment, making divine grace the hinge of the cliff-and-Fire scene.
The section recounts a man speaking about his worldly companion; this verse introduces that remembered companion and supplies the human bond on which the later warning turns.
After the section's account of rescue from the Fire, the speaker asks whether they are not dead; this begins the rescued believers' reflection on the outcome their companion denied.
The section sets a denier's fate against the Lord's saving favor; this continuation says their only death was the first and they are not being punished, completing the contrast in their own words.
The section makes rescue from the Fire depend on the Lord's favor; the next declaration calls this the great triumph, naming the consequence of that rescue.

The section ends with the one who sought the Lord's face attaining contentment; this continuation tells hearers to work toward the just-described triumph, linking the scene to the surah's divergent striving.

The section joins a brink, divine favor, rescue, and guidance; this verse says the believers stood at the edge of a pit of Fire, were rescued from it, and became brothers, making communal reconciliation another form of grace that turns people from the brink.

The section sets Musa and Harun before Pharaoh and gives them a greeting of peace for the one who follows guidance (السَّلَامُ عَلَى مَنِ اتَّبَعَ الْهُدَى); this is the first half of the encounter where guidance and turning away divide outcomes.
The section links 92:16's denial and turning away to the opposite of the guided path; Musa and Harun's warning here places punishment on whoever denies and turns away (كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ).
The section frames the palace encounter as a contest over who gives and rules; Pharaoh's question, “Who is your Lord?”, makes that disputed lordship explicit before Musa answers.

The section says Musa's answer gathers the surah's creating, giving, and guiding into one statement; this verse says the Lord gave each thing its created form and then guided it, bringing those acts together against Pharaoh's claim.

The section's rejected warning culminates in denial and turning away; this preceding act says Pharaoh denied the sign and disobeyed, sharing the source-section's denial root ك ذ ب and establishing the choice before his boast.
The section describes turning one's back from warning; this verse says Pharaoh turned away and hurried on (تَوَلَّىٰ), echoing the source section's 92:16 wording for refusal.

The section contrasts the Lord who gives with a king who claims height for himself; Pharaoh's boast أَنَا رَبُّكُمُ الْأَعْلَىٰ reverses the source-section wording رَبِّهِ الْأَعْلَىٰ, exposing the king's false claim to the elevation belonging to God.
The section says the king who claimed to be highest is brought low; this verse says God seized Pharaoh with punishment in this life and the next, completing the reversal of his boast.
The section's warned hearer may read the Fire as a sign and step aside; this story is explicitly called a lesson for whoever fears, clarifying who can receive the warning.
The section quotes Pharaoh's claim of supreme lordship; this immediately preceding verse has him gather and call out, showing the public act that carries the boast into the encounter.

The section describes the one who holds to worldly wealth and turns from the warning; this verse names the person who transgresses and prefers the nearer life, identifying the choice behind that refusal.
The section contrasts the miser's path with the pious person's; this verse assigns Hell as the abode of the one who prefers worldly life, making the consequence explicit.
The section says the warned person may fear and withdraw from the Fire; this verse describes the one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains his soul from desire, the contrary response.
The section associates fear with being kept away from the Fire; this verse places the self-restrained person's destination in the Garden, completing the opposite outcome to the worldly-life chooser.
The section contrasts two ways and their ends; this closing line names the Garden as the refuge of the one who feared his Lord, finishing the paired warning.
The section's night-path scene turns a warning into a sign for the attentive; this command to remind if the reminder benefits supplies the same admonitory stance.
The section says the warning is a guide for the one who fears; this verse says the reminder will be heeded by the one who fears, directly identifying the responsive listener.
The section says the heedless one ignores the warning and enters the Fire; this verse sets the most wretched person against the fearful listener as the one who avoids the reminder.
The section's heedless person plunges into the blazing Fire; this verse gives the avoider of reminder the great Fire as his outcome.
The section contrasts the Fire with the saved person's contentment; this continuation says the one in it neither dies nor lives, specifying the lasting condition on the warned-against path.
The section links giving and purification with being kept clear of the Fire; this verse says the one who purifies himself prospers, the other path's direct counterpart.

The section joins giving to a face sought for God's sake; this verse associates the successful person's purification with remembering the Lord's name and prayer, extending the image from hand to devotion.
The section depicts the miser's refusal as a preference for immediate possessions; this verse states directly that people prefer the nearer life (تُؤْثِرُونَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا).
The section's giver seeks an enduring divine reward beyond worldly repayment; this verse says the Hereafter is better and more lasting, explaining that choice.

The section joins turning the face, giving wealth, freeing necks, truthfulness, and piety; this verse assembles those same acts, while saying outwardly turning the face east or west is not itself righteousness.

The section's giver seeks God's face without asking people for return; this verse forbids following charity with reminders or injury and promises reward without fear, distinguishing the open hand from a self-serving one.

The section contrasts the high garden that flourishes after rain with the falling ravine; this verse's charity-for-show is like soil washed off bare rock by rain, a precise reversal where the gift leaves no lasting fruit.
The section quotes the high garden hit by a downpour and yielding double fruit; this verse stages that scene and ties its abundance to spending in search of God's approval.

The source section's wording وَجْهِ رَبِّهِ in 92:20 names the giver's sought face; this verse says charity is for seeking Allah's face (لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ) and its full reward, making the refusal of human repayment a positive aim.

The section opens with night covering and day appearing, then divides human striving; this verse names people who give by night and day, in secret and in public, and promises them security, joining the time-image to the giving path.

The section opposes giving to hoarding; this verse uses the source-section root ب خ ل for those who withhold what God gave them and says it will be wrapped around their necks, turning retained wealth into a fitting burden.

The section contrasts the hand that gives with the one that is miserly and describes brothers; this verse praises people who prefer others over themselves and says whoever is protected from stinginess of soul succeeds, directly meeting both motifs.
The section quotes feeding people purely for God's face; this preceding verse shows who receives the food—the needy, orphan, and captive—and that it is given despite being loved.

The section explicitly quotes this declaration of feeding “for the face of Allah” and refusing repayment; its wording لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ and لَا نُرِيدُ مِنكُمْ جَزَاءً matches the source section's hand-and-face meeting.
The section's giver acts with fear of the severe Day; this next line gives that fear as the reason for their unreturned feeding.
The section says the one who fears has a shield and is kept away from evil; this verse says God protected these givers from the evil of that Day, making the shield a concrete act.
The section contrasts the giver's protected path with the Fire and describes a fruitful high garden; this continuation repays patience with a Garden and silk, showing the positive end of giving.
The section opposes giving to withholding; this man promises لَنَصَّدَّقَنَّ if given from God's bounty, using the same giving root ء ت ي as source-section 92:18 يُؤْتِي مَالَهُ.

The section describes one who clutches wealth and turns his back; after receiving bounty, these people become miserly and turn away, repeating the source-section's give/withhold and turn-away pattern.

The section says their vow and later conduct put giving and turning away in one story; this continuation says breaking the promise and lying leaves hypocrisy in their hearts, naming the lasting consequence of that reversal.

The section's branded miser is introduced by this warning against hoarding gold and silver without spending in God's way; the next verse supplies the brand, while this one identifies the stored wealth and refusal.
The section contrasts the pious person kept from harm with the hoarder whose flanks are branded; this verse makes the held gold and silver into the heated iron that brands forehead, sides, and back.

The section puts the high garden of taqwa against a structure on a ravine's edge that collapses into Hell; this verse depicts exactly that unstable foundation and fall, marking the boundary between the two builds.

The section says God provides guidance and people take divergent paths; this verse says the human being has been shown the two roads, making divergence the starting point for the following ascent and outcomes.
The section's cliff-edge and path imagery meets this verse's difficult ascent (الْعَقَبَةَ), a demanding course rather than mere outward direction.
The section's steep edge and descent into Fire make the ascent image legible; this verse asks what the difficult ascent is, introducing the concrete deeds in the next lines.
The section cites freeing necks as a mark of goodness; this verse names freeing a neck (فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ) as the first act of the difficult ascent.
The section joins spending with care for people; this verse adds feeding on a day of hunger as part of the upward path.
The section's righteousness includes support for vulnerable people; this line specifies an orphan near of kin among those fed on the ascent.
The section's giving path includes the needy; this line specifies a poor person in misery as another recipient on the ascent.
The section has the believer use the warning as guidance and follow a protective path; this verse adds mutual exhortation to patience and mercy as the way's communal conduct.
The section sets giving and piety on one path and withholding on another; this verse calls the people of that demanding, merciful path companions of the right.
The section's rejected warning ends in Fire; this verse gives the opposite group the name companions of the left after the ascent passage's deeds.
The section's denier enters the blazing Fire; this verse says the companions of the left are enclosed in a Fire, closing the path-parable with the matching outcome.
The section describes divergent striving and a final meeting with the Lord; this verse says each person is laboring toward the Lord and will meet Him, joining effort to the coming judgment.
The section's giver is kept from harm and reaches contentment; this verse gives the record in the right hand as the opening sign of the favorable outcome.
The section contrasts ease for one path with difficulty for the other; this verse says the right-handed person will have an easy reckoning, completing the favorable side.
The section ends with the saved person attaining satisfaction; this verse's right-handed person returns to his people joyful, a close parallel for that glad outcome.
The section's second path turns its back on warning; this verse places the record behind the back, a concrete image of rejection and opposite fate.
The section says worldly wealth cannot avail the one who falls; after the record is put behind his back, this person cries out for destruction as the account is exposed.
The section contrasts the one kept from Fire with the denier who enters it; this verse sends the back-handed person into a Blaze, completing the same two-outcome pattern.
The section's warning culminates in people entering the Fire; this question names Saqar and invites the condemned to explain how they arrived there.
The section sets the giving, pious person against the one turned away; this answer says the condemned were not among those who prayed, beginning their account of the opposite path.
The section's righteous giver gives without repayment; this answer says the condemned did not feed the poor, naming the direct charitable reversal.
The section contrasts truthful warning with denial; this answer says the condemned joined in vain talk, a neighboring account of how they treated the reminder.
The section traces the fire-bound path to denial; this answer says they denied the Day of Recompense, identifying what they rejected.
The section's plunge comes when wealth no longer avails; this answer says the condemned persisted until certainty came, completing their account of delay.

The section centers on a man recalling his worldly companion; this garden owner boasts to his companion of having more wealth and stronger support, staging a close counterpart to the proud worldly bond.
The section's companion mocks belief and resurrection; this garden owner says he does not think the Hour will come, making the same disbelief concrete in a second companion scene.
The section contrasts the Lord's giving with a person's pride; the companion here answers by recalling creation from dust and a drop, redirecting wealth-boasting to the Creator.
The section's giver seeks the face of the Lord above; this companion declares his Lord is Allah and refuses association, opposing the garden owner's self-confidence.
The section says wealth will not avail when its owner falls; this garden owner's crop is destroyed and he wrings his hands over what he spent, showing worldly possession collapsing.
The section's worldly companion cannot truly secure his friend; this verse says the garden owner has no group to help him apart from God, exposing the limit of human backing.
The section's rescue and favor belong to the Lord; after the garden's ruin, this verse says true protection and reward belong to God, resolving the companion story on that basis.
The section separates bounty from a human claim to favor; this verse depicts a person taking abundance as proof that his Lord honored him, exposing the mistaken worldly reading of wealth.
The section sets the wealthy holder beside the giver; this verse shows the same person treating reduced provision as humiliation, the opposite mistaken reading of God's test.
The section's righteousness is measured by giving, not merely possession; this verse says the wealthy fail to honor the orphan, naming the neglect behind their self-assessment.
The section makes feeding part of the giving path; this verse says the people do not urge one another to feed the poor, an exact contrary social act.
The section opposes giving to grasping wealth; this verse says they consume inheritance greedily, showing possession become appropriation.
The section's miser holds wealth as though it sufficed; this verse names their intense love of wealth, exposing the attachment behind withholding.
The section ends on contentment after the night gives way to an opened face; this verse addresses the tranquil soul and calls it back to its Lord.
The source section's final word is رَضِيَ in 92:21; this verse's رَاضِيَةً مَرْضِيَّةً develops the same satisfaction as both the servant's contentment and God's approval.
The section's saved person reaches the Lord's favor; this continuation invites that soul among God's servants, giving belonging as part of the reward.
The section contrasts the Fire with the seeker's final contentment; this verse ends the tranquil-soul passage with entry into the Garden, the destination that completes that contrast.
The section's warning Fire divides the two kinds of striving; this verse names the Blaze as the rejected person's end.
The section places turning away beside entry into the Fire; this continuation describes that Blaze as stripping the scalp, sharpening the warning's consequence.
The section repeatedly pairs denial with turning away; this verse says the Fire calls the one who turned back and turned away (أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ), echoing the source section's 92:16 تَوَلَّىٰ.
The section's miser clutches wealth and finds it cannot help him; this verse adds the one who gathered wealth and hoarded it to those the Fire calls.
The section's good hand gives wealth; this verse describes the faithful as assigning a known share of their wealth to the asker and deprived person, specifying the contrary use.
The section's righteous giver directs wealth beyond himself; this line identifies the recipients of that share, the asker and the deprived, completing the contrast with hoarding.
The section says worldly wealth will not avail the person who falls; this verse depicts the one who amasses wealth and repeatedly counts it, the possession pattern behind that failure.
The section shows the miser's held wealth failing him; this verse states his false belief that wealth will make him last forever, exposing why he clings to it.
The section's warning ends in a plunge into Fire; this verse says the wealth-counter will be thrown into the Crusher, enacting that fall.
The section's fire image carries both warning and consequence; this question introduces the description of the Crusher that follows.
The section contrasts guiding fire at a distance with the Fire entered by the heedless; this verse identifies the Crusher as God's kindled Fire.
The section says the other Fire reaches the one who plunges in; this verse says the Crusher penetrates to the hearts, making its inward reach explicit.
The section's rejected one is enclosed in the Fire; this verse says the Fire is closed over them, reinforcing the image of no escape.
The section contrasts an open sign-fire with entered punishment; this final image of extended columns completes the Crusher's enclosing scene.
The section makes feeding and care part of righteousness; this verse describes the opposite action of harshly repulsing the orphan.
The section includes feeding others for God's face; this verse condemns failing even to urge the feeding of the poor, reversing that hand-to-mouth scene.
The section says outward orientation alone is not goodness; this verse begins a warning against prayer without its moral substance.
The section distinguishes a true reminder from disregard; this verse describes prayer performed heedlessly, an outward act detached from attention.
The section's giver acts without seeking thanks or return; this verse condemns people who act to be seen, the contrary motive.
The section contrasts open-handed giving with hoarding; this verse ends by condemning those who withhold even small assistance.
The section contrasts the one who clings to worldly property with the one who trusts lasting reward; this verse says whoever wants the immediate life is given some of it and then faces Hell.
The section's giver strives for the Lord's pleasure; this verse pairs desire for the Hereafter with the striving appropriate to it.

The section's palace dialogue distinguishes the Lord who provides from the king who claims dominion; this verse says God's bounty reaches both groups, adding that worldly provision alone does not mark the final path.
The section says night veils human striving and day reveals it; this verse calls night and day signs and makes the visible day a means of seeking bounty and counting time.
The section's opening night covers people's course; this verse uses the same clothing image, جَعَلْنَا اللَّيْلَ لِبَاسًا, making concealment a repeated Quranic scene.
The section pairs covered night with the day that lays striving open; this next verse says daylight is made for livelihood, supplying the contrasting activity.
The section gives night and day opposite roles in the divided course of life; this verse pairs night as covering and sleep as rest with day as a time of rising.

The section sets a fire approached for guidance against the Fire entered by the heedless; Musa says he may find guidance at the fire (هُدًى), making the approached fire a sign rather than a punishment.
The section says Musa's fire is approached as a source of guidance; this continuation has him arrive at the fire and hear the call that begins divine instruction.
The section's guiding fire leads Musa to a message; this call marks the ground as sacred and directs him to remove his sandals, showing the encounter's reverent threshold.
The section's fire is the scene where guidance is found; this continuation says God chose Musa and orders him to listen, identifying the guidance received there.
The section makes the fire an occasion of warning and orientation; Musa is told here that God is his Lord and to establish prayer for His remembrance.

The section explicitly connects the root ص ل ي in source-section 92:15's يَصْلَىٰهَا with this fire Musa approaches to warm himself (تَصْطَلُونَ); the shared root makes one fire warm at a safe distance and the other burn when entered.
The section contrasts an approached sign-fire with the Fire of punishment; at Musa's fire this verse announces blessing for those present, completing the welcoming rather than punishing side.
The section says the fire-path yields guidance; this continuation identifies the caller as Allah, the Mighty and Wise, making the source of that guidance explicit.
The section develops Musa's family traveling at night and his hope of finding fire or guidance; this verse repeats the journey, the distant fire, and his instruction to the family to wait.
The section uses Musa's fire as a source of direction; this continuation calls to him from the tree in the blessed valley, where he receives the divine address.
The section treats Musa's fire as useful and warning fire at once; this question begins another Quranic reflection on fire by asking about what people kindle.
The section says an approached fire may warm and guide; this verse asks whether people created its tree or God did, placing useful fire within divine provision.
The section's fire is a sign on the night path; this verse calls fire a reminder and provision for travelers, directly meeting the signal and usefulness in the image.
The section opposes the Lord who gives to Pharaoh as a king who holds dominion; Pharaoh boasts of Egypt and its rivers as possessions, making earthly rule his counterclaim.
The section contrasts divine giving with a king's self-exaltation; Pharaoh follows his boast by belittling Musa as weak and unclear, showing how the claim is used against the messenger.
The section exposes the king's confusion of wealth with true elevation; Pharaoh asks why Musa lacks gold bracelets and angelic company, treating possessions as proof of rank.
The section contrasts a fruitful high garden tied to giving with wealth held back; this parable begins with garden owners tested by their crop, another meeting of provision and moral choice.
The section's charitable path releases wealth; these garden owners resolve not to give a share to the poor, making their withheld crop the opposite of the giver's hand.
The section's high garden thrives through rain; this garden is struck by a visitation from the Lord while its owners sleep, turning expected yield into loss.
The section's garden imagery distinguishes flourishing from collapse; this continuation says the crop became like something harvested, completing the loss.
The section's giver directs goods outward; these owners set out saying no poor person should enter the garden, specifying their exclusion.
The section's moral hand gives rather than hoards; this verse says the owners go early with the intention of preventing anyone from benefiting, carrying their withholding into action.
The section's Garden imagery joins abundance to right conduct; after finding the crop destroyed, the owners realize they were deprived, the reversal of their expected abundance.
The section ties abundance to the Lord's gift; this garden's owners confess God's perfection and their own wrongdoing after their plan fails.
The section's giving path seeks the Lord's pleasure; the repentant garden owners hope their Lord will replace the lost crop with something better.
The section contrasts the garden that flourishes with the ravine that falls; this parable closes by naming worldly punishment greater, extending the scene to accountability.

The section says the giving hand seeks the Lord's face rather than human repayment; this verse commands giving relatives, needy people, and travelers their due, calling that better for those seeking God's face.
The section contrasts human repayment with the Lord's lasting reward; this verse says wealth gained through usury does not grow with God, while charity seeking His face is multiplied.
The section says the giver has no human favor to repay and seeks the Lord's face; this verse casts spending as a good loan to God, who multiplies it, making the ultimate return divine.
The section's rejected human repayment is paired with seeking the Lord's approval; this verse likewise asks who will lend God a good loan and promises its multiplication.
The section divides the giver from the one who is miserly; this verse says those who withhold only withhold from themselves, clarifying the cost of holding back.
The section's miser is marked by the root ب خ ل; this verse names those who are miserly and hide God's bounty, pairing the same withholding with concealment.

The section contrasts God as giver with human reluctance to release wealth; this verse says that even owners of the treasuries of their Lord's mercy would hold back for fear of spending, making the human grip the counter-image to God's provision.
The section opposes the one who turns away from warning to the one kept from Fire; this verse describes the deniers with blackened faces on Resurrection Day and names Hell as their home.
The section says the God-fearing are kept away from the Fire; this verse says God saves those who feared Him and evil does not touch them, giving the protective side of the contrast.
The section's true giver refuses to seek thanks; this verse says a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, clarifying what makes giving fit for the sought face.

The section's high garden bears abundant fruit after rain; this neighboring garden parable imagines destructive weather striking an owner who is old and has vulnerable children, making the fruitful garden's security a consequential contrast.
The section contrasts a stable garden with a structure that collapses; this parable describes a good word as a good tree with a firm root, giving another image of grounded growth.
The section's garden receives rain and yields doubled fruit; this continuation says the good tree gives fruit continually by its Lord's leave, echoing durable yield.
The section contrasts the secure garden with a ravine-edge structure that falls; this paired parable sets the bad word as a tree uprooted from the earth without stability.

The section's garden rises and produces, while its final reward outlasts worldly possession; this verse's rain-grown vegetation pleases briefly before drying and crumbling, clarifying how worldly abundance can pass.

The section uses the rescued believers' brotherhood as a sign of grace; this continuation has later believers ask that their hearts be free of rancor toward those who came before, extending that reconciled bond.

The section contrasts a structure founded on taqwa with one that collapses into Hell; this verse identifies the opposing mosque built for harm, disbelief, and division, supplying the bad intention behind the unstable foundation in the next ayah.

The section sets the ravine-edge building against one founded on taqwa and seeking God's approval; this neighboring verse explicitly says the mosque founded on taqwa from the first day is more worthy, completing the positive side of the contrast.
The section's rejected hearer turns his back on the warning; this verse describes a man who turned away and became arrogant, the action immediately preceding his sentence to Saqar.
The section pairs denial and turning away with entry into the Fire; following the arrogant man's rejection, this verse says he will be made to enter Saqar, completing that warning scene.

The section sets the Lord who gives against Pharaoh's claim to be the highest ruler; this verse says sovereignty is God's to grant or take away, and honor or abase, exposing the king's claimed height as borrowed and temporary.

The section opens with night covering and day appearing, then speaks of the Lord who creates and gives; this verse joins night entering day with bringing life from death and providing without measure, meeting those images in one statement.
The section contrasts a king's temporary claim to elevation with God's lasting dominion; this verse says everyone on earth passes away, establishing what cannot remain.

The source section's wording وَجْهِ رَبِّهِ (92:20) makes the sought divine face central; this verse says the face of the Lord remains, joining that face to the passage's contrast between what passes and what endures.

The section says Musa's answer gathers creation, giving, and guidance; this continuation of the answer names the Lord who makes the earth a resting place, lays paths through it, sends water, and brings out plants, illustrating provision and direction.
The section's palace answer identifies the Lord as giver; this next verse tells people to eat and pasture their livestock from what God has provided, making the provision concrete.

The section's palace encounter contrasts God's guidance with denial and turning away; after Musa's answer, this verse says Pharaoh was shown every sign but denied them and refused, repeating the denial root ك ذ ب.

The section says no human favor can be repaid and worldly wealth will not save its owner; this verse calls people to spend before a Day with no bargaining, friendship, or intercession, directly joining giving to the limit of earthly ties.
The section's high garden yields double fruit after a downpour; this verse uses seed that multiplies manyfold as a likeness for spending in God's way, linking giving to fruitful increase.
The section describes wealth given for God's face; this verse says righteousness is not attained until one spends from what one loves, clarifying the cost and quality of the open hand.

The section says wealth cannot help once its owner falls; this verse has the dying person ask for a brief delay so he can give charity and become righteous, showing the moment when withheld time and wealth can no longer be recovered.
The section places the failure of wealth at the moment of falling; this continuation says God does not delay a soul when its appointed time comes, completing the urgency of the preceding plea.
The section pairs night that covers with day that appears; this verse swears by the day as it displays, repeating the disclosure side of that image in a passage about the soul's moral outcome.

The section's opening night veils the course of human striving; this paired oath names the night as it covers (وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا يَغْشَاهَا), repeating the concealment image before the passage turns to purification and failure.
